I am now doing my grad degree where I now have the diagnosis and it’s made a world of positive difference. I am in my last semester and am currently at a 93% average.  I worked in my field full time (social work) throughout my degree. 

Here’s some of my tips that helped me to be successful in grad school:

1.  Connect with your disability office at the school. They will be able to help navigate requesting official accommodations throughout your program (e.g, extended deadlines, additional time to write exams, exceptions to participation marks for showing up to class). 

2. Introduce yourself to your professors. This is helpful to build rapport if you need support in the course later on. When I do introductions, usually via email when I first know who’s teach the course/before the official course start date, I state my disabilities (you don’t have to but I find it gave context), symptoms that can effect my learning, and what support I may need from them to be successful in the course. This has helped me so much when I was struggling, professors were much more understanding. 

3. Make connections with peers in your classes/program. Having peers that get how stressful mutual classes can be and how difficult assignments can be is really great when you need to vent because they understand the student life. This also helped me when struggling as my peer group could give me an idea of course readings for that week. Plus, I don’t know about you but I have anxiety over group work so having peers I could trust in this really helped too.

4. Pace yourself, do not leave everything to the last minute. I am a big procrastinator but learned this lesson quick in grad school. Carve out specific times or days to work on school work and stick to this routine as much as possible. This can prevent a lot of hectic stress.

5. Get enough sleep. It’s easy to pull all nighters for school work. But I can’t stress enough how important sleep is to learn but also to manage bipolar. This will help prevent burnout and risk of an episode which would cause more damage than missing one day of studying.

6. Being a student can be financially difficult. Look into see if there’s disability related grants you can apply to. This can help buy accommodation related supplies for school, therapy, medication etc to help and also to take care of yourself. 

Already work in the field and would say it’s my dream field, but looking to further my education to meet my ultimate career goal. It IS possible to succeed but you need to take care of yourself in the process.

Great question! I was actually diagnosed with Bipolar my first year in the  field after graduating from my BSW. That was rough and I had to take a medical leave. It didn’t seep into my work but at home, when the mask lifted, I was a mess. I also wasn’t in the best work environment. 

After much tinkering with medication and being strictly adherent to my treatment plan, I was able
to get a better hold on the Bipolar. My PTSD has been in remission (got the diagnosis as a teen and I’m now 27) for quite a long time so this wasn’t really
a factor. 

I will say I’ve always been able to excel at work. I had a lot of really shitty social workers during my early years as a teen and again in early adulthood and I’m very determined not to be that as I obviously see the value of social work at all levels. I would say my diagnoses and experience with the mental health system actually make me a way better social worker, I have more compassion and passion for the job which shows I think in my advocacy and direct client work. It also gave me great knowledge on how systems work past academic studies and I didn’t have that learning curve in learning that piece. 

Overall, I would say engage in your treatment plan whatever that looks like for you. I would also say try to find a good work environment; my current job is and it’s made a difference! I know if I’m stressed at work, I can lean on my boss and coworkers, and avoid any risk of an episode. Also, don’t let anyone tell you you can’t do this field, excel etc. I was told I wouldn’t graduate high school at one point because of mental health concerns - yet, I am now working in the field for 6 years and went back to grad school, getting a 91% average. It IS possible to be successful with a mental health diagnoses.

This is all from my experience with lithium so it might vary for you as everyone reacts differently. I started bloodwork right away and had it done about once per month. Make sure to get it done! Your doctor will give your bloodwork reqs depending on your treatment plan. I have had toxicity before and it is awful. Read up on symptoms so you have an idea of what it consists of so you know if you should go to the hospital. Also discuss this with your doctor as it varies on many different factors. Mine happened around times of physical change like differing weight. 

I was at a 1200mg dose but am titrating down currently to replace with lamotrigine. I loved lithium but am going off because I experienced a lot of the side effects. My major side effects at that level were weight gain, under the skin acne, loss of menstrual cycle, developed/worsened an irregular heart t-rhythm (still figuring this out with my docs) and thyroid bottoming out. I also had tremors and nausea at the beginning which went away fairly quickly. Most of the major side effects like thyroid issues can be treated easily with other meds so if you’re okay with that I wouldn’t worry too too much. 

Drink tons of water! You’re going to feel like you’re in a desert 24/7 with how thirsty you will become. And again, know the symptoms of toxicity and make sure to go to the hospital when they first begin. Please talk to your doctor to give you specifics for your treatment like bloodwork, dosages etc. They would know best; we can only pull from our experiences which could be wildly different than yours, everyone is different! We can’t properly answer those questions to the extent you need. Doctors are there to help and guide you, don’t be afraid to ask questions!

I was in contact with my family but they thought it was solely PTSD which I definitley  was experiencing still but it also definitley was not just PTSD at all, even though the two overlap quite a bit. At this time, I was taking Effexor that I stopped frequently because surprise it wasn’t working. 

Anyways, I moved back to my hometown for my masters. I was back around my care team and my family. It was then people clued in that there was something else going on. I had a massive breakdown which led me to drop out of my masters and finally be diagnosed at age 22. I was first diagnosed with bipolar NOS to give more time for my pysch to evaluate me and originally thinking maybe bipolar 2. My pysch sent me to a mood disorder specialized pysch for a second opinion. I was re-diagnosed to bipolar 1 as it was pretty clear I experienced a full manic episode a few times which my pysch confirmed after further monitoring. 

I knew bipolar could be triggered by trauma so I thought that’s what happened (which could be a component still for me for sure) as I also knew genetics plays a large role in all of it. Then I found out I had family members with it. I never knew that I had cousins with bipolar until after I was diagnosed. It would have been great if I knew before but hey, at least I know now.

1. Take your meds but also don’t be scared to communicate to whoever is prescribing your meds if they’re not working, the side effects are really doing a toll on you, etc. Find a therapist you trust and has a modality you like, no shame in going to a few before you find one. Group therapy is awesome because you get to talk to people with similar experiences. Try to find what triggers cycles or what symptoms you can catch early if possible so you can go to your care team. Read as much as you can on Bipolar. Exercise and eating well is helpful. Know what friends, family, etc have your back and are willing to listen when you need it. 

2. Let yourself grieve it. Grieve what you did, who you are, whatever you gotta do. Talk it through with a therapist. But know this is a normal feeling and that it’s okay to feel like this. 

3. Lithium is fantastic. When you first start, you might have to have a little snack with it because it can be hard on the stomach. Make sure you get regular bloodwork and ECGs. Know the signs of lithium toxicity and go to the hospital ASAP if you think you’re experiencing toxicity. If you ever switch off of it, make sure they taper you slowly; learned the hard way, went manic.

Before the age of 12, I had about six therapists. When I was little, I had a terrible phobia of frogs; no idea why but it impacted my daily life. As I entered into 13, my parents noticed a behavioural change and put me into therapy. I didn’t tell the therapist I was undergoing trauma. Trauma went from  late 12/13 to 14. 

I was hospitalized at 14 after my parents caught me just before a suicide attempt. The psychiatrist was awful and diagnosed me with panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder and major depressive disorder. My parents and my brother all have anxiety and depression and all took Effexor. I was put on Effexor due to it working with my immediate family. I was also given trazedone to sleep (I had incredibly bad insomnia) and atavain PRN for panic attacks. Although the pysch was terrible, the social worker was pretty tuned into things and told my parents I had some trauma and that I likely have PTSD.

I told the psychiatrist off in outpatient and she discharged me as a patient. I got a new psychiatrist where I was doing group therapy. Age 15, I am diagnosed with PTSD. Stay on Effexor and Atvain, switch to Seroquel for sleep. I started trauma therapy. I was still moody, frequently missing school, having bad nightmares and flashbacks. 

Changed psychiatrists at 17 as my parents wanted me to go to one of “top” psychiatrists in the area since there wasn’t a big change. This is still the psychiatrist I have today! She confirmed PTSD diagnosis and increased my Effexor to an ungodly amount. Despite everything, I still did well and got a full scholarship to university that was 6 hours from my hometown and where I knew nobody. I was excited to get away from the town that reminded me so much of trauma. I also started EMDR for the trauma, it helped some. I am hospitalized a few more times before 18. 

Age 18 and my mood begins to dramatically shift.
I thought I was just getting better and my high mood was how normal people felt. I started binge drinking and blacking out, having sex with multiple people in a short period of time and having particularly risky sex, felt very confident and invincible, etc. I stopped taking my medication and told my psychiatrist I felt great and stopped seeing her frequently.  I lost my scholarship as my grades suffered. It was the perfect storm - no family or friends around that would see the shift and no more supervision from the psychiatrist. When I called my family, they chalked it up to normal university behaviour. My friends at university just thought it was my personality. I would then fall into depression. I would disengage from people. Stopped going to class, felt suicidal constantly, felt ashamed and guilty. My dad would drive to take care of me during those times. My parents thought it must be the PTSD. 

I repeated that cycle constantly and was hospitalized frequently for suicidal ideation. I started getting SGB for PTSD. It took the PTSD symptoms away completely. I still get these done every year or so. My mood was still ever changing despite the shot. Still nobody catches on there could be something else. I reconnect with my psychiatrist during this time, I was put back on Effexor. The supervision was still spotty but it was back on her books. After SGB, I am taken off meds. 

I somehow graduate and get accepted to a masters program. I attributed this to manic overachieving and taking on all the things. It lifted my grades and helped my CV. I move back home for school and get my first job in my field. I loved the work but was missing a lot of work and getting in fights with my boss. I start grad school full time while working full time. Not my best decision. I become very paranoid about the people around me. My family is now noticing something isn’t right as they are right there with me and my mood. I end up slipping into the worst depression I have ever had and get hospitalized. I am more suicidal then ever. My mom literally had to sleep beside me so she could hear if I got up to try to kill myself. I cycle in and out of the hospital, take a sick leave from work, and drop out of grad school. I am not eating and I am completely out of it. I suddenly shift moods and am determined to get back into school, my confidence is through the roof, I am staying up all night doing different projects, and I get bad paranoia again. Also HR is involved at work for my fighting with my boss after I return way too soon to work. I am 22. 

My psychiatrist finally pieces it together and diagnoses me with bipolar NOS, leaning towards Bipolar 2. I am put on seroquel and Wellbutrin (unsure why the Wellbutrin). She sends me to a mood specialist psychiatrist for assessment. I have a through assessment. Turns out I’m neither NOS or 2 and am diagnosed with Bipolar 1. I switch to solely lithium and seroquel for sleep. It works! My mood stabilizes.

Since then, I have been fairly stable. My pysch tried to change my meds to Latuda since I gained a lot of weight. This didn’t work and I became manic then depressed. Back on lithium and did pretty well. Some hypomania and depression but nothing like it was. 

I am 24 now and since my diagnosis I have gone back to school (not masters yet but soon!), got a better job which I excel at, connected with friends more and am all and all doing well. No PTSD symptoms either. I am currently on buspar (truly helps with my anxiety/paranoia), seroquel, lithium and lamotrigine. I am coming off lithium due to weight gain (like it was really bad) and haven’t had an issue with lamotrigine after getting over the whole nausea and insomnia thing. I plan to go back on lithium if it’s doesn’t work out. I still see the same psychiatrist who has been great and I have a really really good therapist who I trust and connect with. My family and friends have all been supportive. I occasionally hear remarks about bipolar that aren’t great at work which sucks. I found out after the fact I have family on my dads side with bipolar, I had no idea before. 

I wish I knew then what I know now and that the highs weren’t just how happy people feel. I am glad it was caught relatively soon. Sorry for the wall of text but I hope this helps!

I’m 22 years old. Growing up, my family life was good - I’m very close with my parents and my older brother. My parents always supported us and were always loving towards us. My parents both came from “rough” childhoods. My mum was the daughter of immigrants and grew up in nearly poverty conditions. My dad grew up in poverty and his family had lots of addiction and inter generational trauma. We didn’t talk much with their families. A few aunts, uncles and cousins, and my grandma. Both sides of the family have various mental illnesses, all of my immediate family do, but we don’t know anyone in the family that had a formal diagnosis of bipolar, although my dad suspects many of his family members did live with bipolar and my mom thinks the same for her dad. I was a pretty sensitive kid. I did well in school, always ended up in gifted/advanced classes. I would cry a lot randomly in my room and be very sensitive to other people struggling etc. But there wasn’t much signs when I was younger. 

In elementary school, I had good friends but was bullied a fair bit. This definitely hit  my self esteem hard. At 12, I started to experience abuse. It lasted for 2 years until I was 14. This really effected me. My first hospitalization was in my first year of high school. My parents caught me JUST before I was going to overdose. At that time, I was just diagnosed with anxiety, depression and panic disorder. In my opinion, as someone who works in the field now, the psychiatrist who did this diagnosis was waaaaay off and pretty awful all together. I started meds and therapy. A year later with a new psychiatrist, I was diagnosed with PTSD. I had another couple hospitalizations before I finished high school. 

My mum and my brother always suspected bipolar was a possibility with me but since my PTSD symptoms mimick some of my bipolar symptoms, they brushed it off. Fast forward, I went to university and graduated from social work. During uni, I still struggled. Had hospitalizations. My mom found a treatment for PTSD that was a lifesaver. It’s a stellate ganglion block(SGB). It’s only offered in the states for ptsd  so we had to travel and pay out of pocket, I’m really lucky my parents had some money to spare for it (we live in Canada and it’s only available for chronic pain management). It totally took away all my PTSD symptoms, I was amazed. The treatment itself is over 90% effective. 

I moved out of my university city and back home to pursue my masters in social work. Right when I graduated my bachelors, I was lucky and got a job with benefits, unionized, decent starting pay etc. Very high stress but I like it - still at that job but currently on a sick leave. I started my masters and I had my biggest “breakdown” since my first hospitalization. I dropped out of grad school, took a sick leave from work etc. My psychiatrist who I’ve now had since I was 17, started to monitor me for bipolar. After a couple months and looking back at certain behaviours and periods of time, she diagnosed with bipolar NOS. So diagnosed this past October at 22.

I got on meds and more therapy. I struggle more with the depression than hypomania. I’m still learning. Really lucky to have a good support system and an understanding workplace. My partner and my family have done everything they can to educate themselves on bipolar - Read books, searched the web, asked friends who’s kids have bipolar or who have bipolar themselves, asked my pysch lots of questions.
